label: The Cave
take: For her the Allegory of the Cave holds the whole teaching of awakening in one image, and Plato gives it as his answer to what paideia is. She reads the cave as a tomb and also as a womb: leaving it is a birth, with conception, gestation, labour and a midwife. In her reading the prisoners are chained by legs and neck but their hands are free, meaning free will and the heart can never be enslaved. The root cave is not society or even the body but the way an unknowing mind binds itself, and the freed must go back down out of love and justice.

label: Paideia
take: Paideia is not diplomas, rote learning (παπαγαλία) or technical training but the art of turning the whole eye of the soul from outside to inside, from becoming toward being and the Good. She ties the word to παῖς, the child: it is all for the child, the awakening of the sacred child, the eternal being one already is. In society it is the gate that joins the citizen to the polity, which is why every power has wanted to control it. She reads modern Greek resignation partly as the result of paideia being stripped away.

label: Turning of the soul
take: Μεταστροφή is the turn from looking outward to looking inward. You will never find the exit of the cave in the senses or in space and time, where you only bang on the wall and go deeper; you must turn all your attention within. She reads the pandemic as the world forcing this turn on everyone, and the 28 October talk opens by turning attention from a remembered past to the now. What usually sets it off is being fed up with the torment of change.

label: Ever-living fire
take: Reading Heraclitus B30, she holds that the whole cosmos, intelligible, psychic and material, is an ever-living fire that no god or human made, so maker and made are one. This fire is not candle flame or electricity, which are only its reflections in the cave, but Logos, primordial consciousness, which the Platonists call Nous. It is 'kindled in measures and quenched in measures' not like a radiator switched on and off but as manifesting and unmanifest at the same moment, like the frames of a film. In Part B she extends it: justice itself is the finest, fastest fire running through everything.

label: The Good
take: The Good is the first sun, the μέγιστον μάθημα, without which no other learning counts as true knowledge. It is beyond knowledge and truth, so it is touched and lived rather than understood; its light is truth and its heat is eros. In her vocabulary the small word εὖ names this inner light: whatever is joined to it takes on goodness, and diving to one's core one finds that one's being is the Good. Following Plotinus she says that when you know it you recognise it as yourself, and it comes 'like one who never left'.

label: Eudaimonia
take: Eudaimonia is the final cause of all causes: behind every car, marriage or job lies the wish for it, and nothing lies behind it (Aristotle). She defines it as an unshakeable fullness and freedom that depends on no condition, and as recognising your inner fiery δαίμων, which separates it from εὐτυχία, luck that turns with chance's wheel. Security, goods and relationships are conditions for cultivating it, never its source; it comes only from the soul's inward turning, and the awakened work for the εὐδαιμονία of all beings.

label: Heraclitus
take: People call him 'the dark', but she calls him the most luminous philosopher she has met, one you need a 'Delian diver' to reach. She builds whole talks on his fragments: B30 on the ever-living fire, B52 on Aion as a child playing, B118 on the dry soul, the common Logos (ξυνός), and Dionysus and Hades being the same. For her he teaches a radical non-dualism in which the poet and the poem are one.

label: Plato
take: Plato is her main source, read as an initiatory teacher of awakening rather than a builder of abstract systems. She treats the Republic, subtitled 'On the Just', as so complete that if it alone survived it would carry the quintessence of Hellenic philosophy, and its three similes (Sun, Line, Cave) as a staged map of ascent. She also draws on the Phaedo (philosophy as practice of dying), the Symposium (Diotima), the Theaetetus (maieutics), the Timaeus, the Phaedrus and above all the Cratylus for etymologies.

label: Eros
take: Eros, with wonder, is the beginning of philosophy and of all change: to love freedom, true life, the εὖ ζῆν. She derives it from ῥέω, to flow: a cosmic current that passes through you and makes you lose the old false self, which is exactly the point. In the Sun simile eros is the heat of the Good as truth is its light, so the real philosopher is incandescent rather than coldly detached, and the first trait Socrates asks of a philosopher-leader is to be ἐρωτικός. It cannot be engineered with 'five tips'; it is the mystery of the Good, and she separates it sharply from attachment and obsession.

label: Living well
take: Starting from Alexander, who owed ζῆν to his parents and εὖ ζῆν to Aristotle, she defines living well as one's relationship with oneself, not success, money or fame. It means freedom, virtue, inner peace (γαλήνη, ἀταραξία) and care for the common good, and it is a feast to celebrate rather than a life to endure. Paradoxically she calls it the easy path: what is hard is being tossed up and down by every honk and setback. Collective εὖ ζῆν is also the purpose of justice and what the just leader serves.

label: Justice
take: Justice is not 'getting my rights' or punishment but balance held from the middle of Themis's scale, a collective state that brings things back to the mean. Inwardly it is τὰ ἑαυτοῦ πράττειν, each part of the soul doing its own around the one fiery Self, so it is an energy and a state rather than an act. Beyond the cave, in her reading of the Cratylus, justice is the finest, fastest fire passing through all things, the self-regulation of the cosmic fire that keeps the universe balanced. With eros it is one of the two keys to the Good, and it is why the freed must return to the cave.

label: Nous
take: In this talk she uses νοῦς as a near synonym of consciousness and says it can work in five ways, which together make up Plato's theory of knowledge. Her central claim is that there is one wonder-worker, one prisoner, one light and one awakening, and all of them are the nous. With Marcus Aurelius she adds that all people are siblings, children of the same nous.

label: Logos
take: Logos has many meanings she draws out with her audience (cause, ratio, speech, analogy, promise, reckoning), and every vibration of spacetime is a logos, a ratio shaping the energy of the whole. With Heraclitus she insists the Logos is one and common (ξυνός, with upsilon, not ξινός, 'sour'), though most people think they have a private understanding. The fire of Heraclitus is Logos, primordial consciousness, mostly unspoken (ἄρρητος). Politically, following Aristotle, the political is the distinctive property of logos: our capacity to judge just and unjust.

label: Truth
take: Truth for her is simple and has no content: it is a state, not a set of propositions or rules ('not the Ten Commandments'), and propositions are true only by participation (μέθεξις) in it. She reads ἀλήθεια as non-forgetting or non-sleep, hears in 'αλ' a root of light as in ἥλιος, and tentatively sees an anagram of θήλεια, female, because truth keeps giving birth. Truth does not come to you; you come to the truth, which waits here already.

label: Lethe, forgetting
take: Lethe, forgetting, is what the soul drinks on its descent: it falls from the ever-being into the illusion of the body-tomb-cave. The chains of the cave are λήθη, and the prisoners sleep in the cosmic dream. Asked what is opposite to Being, she says nothing is: within Being there is only the possibility of forgetting itself, and Lethe is the price God pays to manifest and play. Truth, which says 'change', is almost unbearable to someone still in λήθη.

label: Second birth of the soul
take: The Orphic, Pythagorean, Eleusinian and Platonic traditions call the awakening of consciousness, while still in the body, a second birth, and she reads Christmas and the ancient Heliougenna as its festival. She maps it as a real pregnancy: a hidden conception below the radar of senses and mind, gestation nourished by love, teaching and virtue, labour pains with a midwife-teacher, a sudden birth into light, then nourishment and strengthening. The newborn is a revelation of what we always were, new and always ancient. Even knowledge follows this pattern: it must be conceived, carried and born in you.

label: The sudden
take: Ἐξαίφνης, Plato's 'suddenly', is her favourite Platonic word in the podcast: the moment the prisoner is released, or the soul is born into light when its hour is ripe. It does not depend on the human mind but on cosmic law (νομοτέλεια); other traditions call it providence, and it belongs to mystery, which holds the highest place in philosophy. It can come as loss, divorce, ruin or depression, or as an inspiration and the love of one's life, a 'good suddenly'. Either way it shakes a boxed, repetitive life awake.

label: Transcendence
take: Transcendence is the first of the two movements of philosophy: closing the eyes (μύω), turning away from becoming and finding the One 'beyond'. She calls the belief that truth lies somewhere else a useful 'intermediate falsehood' that helps the soul turn inward. It corresponds to leaving the cave, deconstructing every conjecture, belief and even idea, up to the mystics' 'devouring fire'. But the soul cannot stay above, so transcendence is only half of initiation.

label: Immanence
take: Immanence is the second and longer movement: returning to the cave to recognise that the One remains in everything, here and now. She glosses ἐμμένεια as ἐν + μένω, the One that dwells everywhere, and illustrates it with Odysseus who, after reaching Ithaca, must still slay the suitors, that is, bring light to old habits and programming and integrate them. In daily life it means seeing the One at the tax office, on Taxisnet, in emails and morning coffee. The freed return out of love and justice and live on the razor's edge of the One and the many.

label: Death and the practice of dying
take: From the One's perspective, birth into the body is a death and physical death is a return. The first definition of philosophy (Phaedo 64) is μελέτη θανάτου, practice of dying, but the death she means is the death of illusion and of the personality, dis-identifying from the body rather than leaving it. It is a daily process, removing one identification at a time, which is why Socrates says both 'dying' and 'being dead'. For those below the freed one has died, for those above he was born, and when he returns he seems risen from the dead.

label: Soul
take: The soul is the vehicle of nous, formed when fiery nous 'cools'; she plays on ψυχή and ψύχω, to cool. It contains the body rather than the reverse: the Timaeus has the soul embracing the body, and what lies outside the body is our aura. In her reading the soul is ἀγαθοειδής, Good-like, carrying a little fiery sun, and in Plato the soul, not the body, is the true subject of politics. It descends by putting on tunics and ascends by taking them off until it is naked.

label: The One
take: The One is the ultimate nature of self and cosmos in the Orphic-Platonic-Pythagorean line she calls ancestral: ineffable (ἄρρητον), unknowable (ἄγνωστον), ungraspable (ἄληπτον) and unparticipated (ἀμέθεκτον). It is not a 'something' but an over-full nothing, a boundless radiance that is transcendent and immanent at once: all is in it and it is in all. It shines through every form like one light through the windows of many rooms, and it waits for us to see it rather than us waiting for it.

label: Know thyself
take: She reads Apollo's Delphic command in two stages. First we take it to mean knowing our personality, preferences, body and the three parts of the soul, and that stage is valid. But at the level of being it asks us to know THE self, which is one in the universe: 'know that which knows', the observer who has thoughts, emotions and a body but is none of them. It is the foundational precept that turns the soul's eye inward, and a life not lit by it is, she says, harder than the effort of self-knowledge.

label: The Sun
take: In her reading of Plato's Sun simile, which she calls 'Platonic trigonometry', the eye is the most sun-like organ and stores the sun's light; likewise the soul is Good-like and carries a small fiery sun within. The sun is self-luminous while objects are lit by another, and it causes growth without being any of them, as the Good causes knowledge. Its light is truth and its heat is eros. The goal is a stability beyond the solstices, the 'ever-living sun', from whose point of view there is no waxing or waning.

label: Light
take: Light is her constant image of spirit: the One is a boundless radiance (φωταύγεια, διαύγεια) that spreads like light through the windows of many rooms while staying one. The soul feeds on light, λόγος and realisations, and words are small vehicles carrying that light. She distinguishes three lights by their roots: sensible (ἡλ-, as in ἥλιος), spiritual (ἑλ-, as in Ἕλλην) and uncreated (the third root is uncertain).

label: Being and non-being
take: Following Parmenides, only what always is, is; for the ancients 'is not' means 'is not true', not 'does not exist'. Whatever rises and sets, sometimes is and sometimes is not, has the quality of non-being: bodies, thoughts, emotions, war and peace, economic booms and busts. Hence Parmenides' reversal: what seems to be is not, and what seems not to be (the invisible, intelligible) truly is. Being has no opposite; being and non-being are not two but one.

label: Becoming
take: Becoming is the realm where nothing stays, so everything dies every moment: we live but do not live. She draws it under a 'T' on the board, below the world of rest, as Plato's world of otherness where the pairs of opposites live, and links it to water and Poseidon, the sea of emotions and beliefs. It is a mirror showing an inverted image, a 'drama of the mind' that sees dualistically. Pain within becoming is the alarm clock telling the soul to change.

label: Philosophy
take: For her, philosophy is a lived spiritual path whose aim is the fulfilment of human nature: to be whole, free and happy. It starts as a love affair, an Eros for truth, and the mind serves only its first steps before it must let go into what contains it; wisdom is not acquired but activated, the clarity of our own being knowing itself. What universities teach today (arguments, polemics, the history of ideas) is in her view only the shell of what its founders defined as a path of awakening.

label: The political
take: For the Greeks politics is human nature, not a contract: we are by nature political animals, and the polis exists by nature, prior even to family and individual. So 'I'm not political' is itself a political stance, a frustration of that nature, and today's depoliticisation goes with a 'de-naturalisation'. Plato's polis mirrors the citizen's soul (her 'psycho-politics'), the lawgiver shapes character, and the true polity's shared purpose is awakening. Real participation means judging and ruling together in spaces of logos, not a four-yearly 'political ritual'.

label: Aristotle
take: Aristotle appears as Alexander's teacher, who gave him εὖ ζῆν, and as the source of her political anthropology: man is by nature a political animal, the polis exists by nature, and the citizen shares in judging and ruling. She uses his principle that science starts from 'what it is' (τί ἐστι), his view that εὖ ζῆν is the purpose of life and of politics, and his claim that the Good moves things 'as the beloved'. She says that for him γενναιότητα is the first moral virtue.

label: Awakening
take: For her the fashionable word 'awakening' belongs to consciousness, not to the body (though it finally includes it) and not even to the soul, whose awakening is only one stage. Reality is already awake as living logos and self-knowing nous; only we sleep and wake, so nothing changes in the world and everything changes in us. It is not a spectacle of visions or miracles but an often unnoticed inner shift of vision, like veils lifting, and she maps it as five ordered steps named after Apollo. In the eros talk the erotic path is itself a path of awakening, which she equates with eudaimonia and freedom.

label: Non-duality
take: She reads the Greek tradition as non-dual: in Plotinus' witness the seer and the seen are one, a union (ἕνωσις) other cultures call yoga. Diotima's negative description of absolute beauty is for her 'a wonderful non-dual description', the most language can do beyond the duality it is built for. She also rejects the dualist Plato in which sensible and intelligible are enemies; for her they are one continuum, and at the deepest level the inside and outside of the cave are one.

label: Winter solstice
take: The winter solstice, when the sun seems to stand still and then climbs again, is for her the soul's deepest dive into the body, the longest night and 'dark night of the soul' before rebirth. Christmas falls four days later because for the Pythagoreans four is establishment, the cube: what was performed in the depths is consolidated. She treats solstices and equinoxes as days of highest energetic inflow around which the ancient festival calendar was built. Yet from the sun's own point of view there is no waxing or waning at all.

label: Body
take: Life in the body is, from the One's view, the field of death: σῶμα σῆμα, the body as tomb, the Cave, the soul's winter solstice. Yet awakening happens without leaving the body, by dis-identifying from it. The body is the vehicle of the soul and is contained by it, not the reverse. Politically she criticises the modern individual understood as a body, the subject of science and biopolitics, set in the place of soul and consciousness.

label: Wisdom
take: Wisdom is living awareness (ἐπίγνωσις) in contact with the here and now, where life itself tells you what is what. Using the Cratylus she ties σοφία to light and to ὁρμή, motion, being connected with an ever-changing energy, and σύνεσις to 'going along with' things like an alert general. The dry soul is the wisest, warmed by the fire of the Good. Pythagoras, she says, knew that love (φιλότης) and wisdom go together.

label: Freedom
take: She asks us to celebrate freedom not as a memory but as the present state of our existence. Splitting ἐλευθερία, with an omega slipped under its omicron, she finds light (Ἑλ), the good (εὖ) and the eros that warms (θέρ-, ἔρως): freedom is eros, which is why a «Yes» must follow the «No». In the other talks freedom is what the free hands of the cave prisoners already hold and what self-inquiry finds at the root of awareness.

label: Free will
take: In her reading the prisoners of the cave are chained by legs and neck but not by the hands, and hands stand for free will, an extension of the heart, which can never be subjugated. So the first ingredient of liberation is wanting it: no mother, partner or child can change you from outside, except perhaps divine grace. 'Even the universe respects free will', so leave the door open a little. Wanting starts to turn the wheels of soul and life and draws events.

label: Respecting shame
take: She offers the Delphic maxim αἰσχύνην σέβου, 'respect shame', as a healthy alternative to self-flagellation, which she calls a pathological relation to conscience. Αἰδώς is the restraint felt before a wrong act, αἰσχύνη what one feels after it; respecting shame means respecting the self-regulation of justice within you. The ego hides from its Erinyes and from solitude; instead one sees the error, learns, adjusts and moves on. Feeling shame is healthy; feeling nothing is the danger.

label: Socrates
take: Socrates' 'I know one thing, that I know nothing' is the method that opens the pores of ἀπορία so Apollo can reveal himself. His daimonion told him only 'make music and work at it', meaning reach the last step of harmonising the many, and he walked the agora as a true political man until pseudo-politicians condemned him. In the eros talk he learns from Diotima, calls the path an erotic pedagogy, and teaches that health is inner peace and illness an inner civil war.

label: Parmenides
take: She calls him 'grandfather Parmenides', near whom Socrates sprouted. From him she takes that only what always is, is, and non-being never was, and the reversal: what seems to be is not, what seems not to be, is. His line 'to think and to be are the same' grounds her view that to be is to be conscious and that we are waves of fire and intellection.

label: Plotinus
take: 'Beloved Plotinus' supplies her key descriptions of awakening: the seer is one with the seen, so it is not even a vision; you do not become someone else, 'another' wrapped around you departs; and the One waits for us to see it. His light passing from room to room images the one essence in many forms, and his 'let us flee to the beloved fatherland' turns the Odyssey into the soul's homecoming. She pairs him with θέασις and θέωσις, and with the call to become σύμπας.

label: Proclus
take: She speaks of 'beloved and fully awakened Proclus'. From him she takes that the soul descends by synthesis, adding foreign tunics, and ascends by analysis, removing what does not belong to it until it is naked (quoting a Chaldean oracle). His procession and return (πρόοδος, ἐπιστροφή) frame her two movements of transcendence and immanence. She also cites his derivation of the Titans from τείνω and, uncertainly, of Dionysus as 'two minds'.

label: Diotima
take: Socrates' teacher, a priestess from Arcadia in her account, and in the Symposium the only surviving text where we see a woman teaching. Diotima defines philosophy as a path of Eros and lays out a ladder of love that Potari counts as seven levels, rising from interpersonal to political and cosmic love. Her erotic pedagogy is for Potari the education every age needs, and she also cleansed the karmic residue of the plague in Athens.

label: Apollo
take: Apollo, god of light and clarity, is for her the god of awakening itself. She builds a whole talk on nine keys: the four etymologies of his name in Plato's Cratylus and the five cult names in Plutarch's On the E at Delphi, read as five ordered steps with the etymologies as the passages between them. Her favourite reading is ἀ + πολλῶν, 'not of the many': he takes no side and removes the poles, and when the many go the One appears. Every etymology of his name, she says, has a subtractive and an additive side.

label: Dionysus
take: Dionysus' birth at the winter solstice (the Dionysia, Heliougenna) is the ancient form of the sacred infant's birth, and Heraclitus says Dionysus and Hades are the same. He holds the initiatory mirror: the visible world is an inverted reflection, and the Titans dismember him as daily pulls fragment our attention. As god of theatre he teaches that each of us plays a role but is not the role. She cites a reading of his name as 'two minds' (δύο νοῦς), the dyadic mind that must pass through the drama.

label: Ares
take: She rescues Ares from the hot-headed war god of popular tales. In his higher form he is the upward impulse of birth (Aries, spring, the shoot breaking the soil) and the power that divides in order to restore justice and good order (εὐταξία). Following Proclus she sets him beside Athena: Athena is war by union at the intelligible level, Ares war by division in the sublunar, emotional world, and wisdom always outranks force. Purified and raised on a base of purity, his red fire becomes vital force, boundaries, health, frank speech and the courage the awakened need in the cave, which is why she calls him the god of peace.

label: Hestia
take: In the Orphic sequence Hestia, read as οὐσία, essence, falls asleep into multiplicity and dreams the incarnation, so life is the divine dream and death its end. She is also the nucleus of Olympus around which Ares forms the outer shell. In the Pythagoras lesson the ἑστία is the sacred fire at the centre of the heart: light it before you speak of sacred things, so that the light becomes words.

label: Aion, the playing child
take: Heraclitus says Aion is a child playing draughts and the kingship is the child's. She reads αἰών as ἀεὶ ὤν, 'the ever-being': the child holds infinite possible scenarios as dice and at each moment manifests a new world or role. This Child was the goal of the Kabeiric mysteries of Samothrace, and the 'kingdom of the child' anticipates the 'kingdom of God'. The reborn soul becomes such a child again, playing freely but wisely, and God forgets himself as a child in order to play and return.

label: Odyssey
take: The Odyssey is her map of the soul's journey home (νόστος), which she pairs with νόστιμος, 'tasty': nothing is tastier than eudaimonia. Odysseus leaves Circe, Calypso and even the advanced Phaeacians, because high understanding is a station, not the goal: 'as long as you see something, you haven't reached Ithaca'. Her twist is that Odysseus does not return to Ithaca; he wakes up in Ithaca, because he was always there.

label: Delphi
take: 'We are the oracle of Delphi': the old, stagnant chthonic forces occupying the sacred space of our soul are the Python in the oracle. At the first step knowledge is still mediated, as when we go to a Pythia who is 'somewhere else'; mantic knowing means becoming the oracle ourselves. There was a lesche at Delphi, the meeting place of the fifth step, and the Delphic γνῶθι σαυτόν names the erotic path.

label: The Mysteries
take: The Orphic, Eleusinian, Kabeiric and Platonic traditions encode the second birth. She derives initiation (μύησις) from μύω, closing eyes and lips to turn inward, and says from μύησις comes κύησις, pregnancy: initiation is conception, gestation, birth. The Kabeiric procession led to 'the Child', Persephone's story traces descent and return, and the Eleusinian climax fell, she says, at the autumn equinox. Mystery holds the highest place in philosophy.

label: Emanation
take: In her simplified Neoplatonic model, matter flows from soul, soul from nous, and nous from the fiery One: one continuum, drawn as a sphere because all cosmogony happens inside the One. Heraclitus has no creation, only manifestation, a moment when something lights up. Each level is a vehicle (ὄχημα) of the one above: body of soul, soul of nous, nous of fire. Every light likewise is an outflow of fire.

label: The dry soul
take: Heraclitus B118 says the dry soul is wisest and best. She explains αὔη as ἀ- plus ὕω, 'not rained upon': the soul warmed by the fire of the Good, truth and Apollo evaporates the passions, which the tradition calls wet and sticky, each passion a κόλλημα, a sticking. Fear, rage, jealousy and envy soak the soul deeper into Poseidon's waters. The remedy is contact with the forms, the inward turn and the cultivation of virtue and justice.

label: Maieutics
take: Socrates' art is midwifery: he speaks only with those already pregnant in soul and helps what is held in potential pass into actuality. The gestation must already have begun in the student; no teacher can do the inner work for you. In the birth of the soul the midwife-teacher pulls one out 'with force' at the ripe hour. Knowledge too is conceived as a seed, carried and delivered with maieutic help.

label: Nikos Kazantzakis
take: She loves Kazantzakis and calls him 'the Heraclitus of the modern era'. His Ascetic, subtitled Salvatores Dei, shows her that the path is warlike: we must save God, the divine spark, from our personality and traumas, and its closing prayer that even the One does not exist marks for her the last step to the Source. In the 28 October talk his sense that 'if the earth is not saved, it is my fault' is what she says Greeks felt in 1940.

label: Pain as a wake-up call
take: Pain, loss and grief in becoming are the soul's alarm clock, signals that something must change. Depression can be 'the cry of the soul' to be freed from the prison it built, a 'spiritual surgery' for someone whose mask has stuck, and its long sleep can be a passage from the sleep of routine to waking; she reframes 'depressed' as 'deep rest'. She speaks of her own loss of a loved one, and adds that help may be needed so the person does not get lost there. One may also need to be 'sufficiently disappointed by becoming' for the flame of eros to catch.

label: Cosmos
take: 'This cosmos, the same for all' in Heraclitus means the totality of creation, every ontological level, and she sees parallel universes already implied. It was made by no god or human: it is self-manifesting fire, beyond space and time. The cosmos is ἔλλογος, rational and conscious, governed by mathematical laws that also govern human becoming, which is why our consciousness is collective. Through justice, the subtlest fire, it is always in balance.

label: Nature
take: Greek ethical and political thought turns on living κατὰ φύσιν, according to nature, in a cosmos that is rational. She diagnoses the last two centuries as a 'de-naturalisation' (ἀποφυσικοποίηση): the belief that we are separate from a non-rational nature, the twin of depoliticisation. For the Greeks all is φύσις, which is why 'metaphysics' is not a Greek category but a library label for Aristotle's work placed after the Physics.

label: Consciousness
take: She reads συνείδησις as σύν + εἰδέναι: being present with the knowing, the seeing and self-knowledge, so that we are συνειδότες, witnesses of truth. Consciousness works like a searchlight: wherever its beam turns, it receives that experience. The essence of the world is already consciousness of itself, Aristotle's νόησις νοήσεως, so awakening is our consciousness turning toward what already is. Its clarity, our 'tuning', decides how the god appears to us.

label: Virtue
take: Following an etymology she takes from Plato's Cratylus, she reads ἀρετή as 'ever-flowing' (ἀεὶ ῥεῖν): virtue is the soul's energy flowing freely, without blockages. Observing and knowing the soul restores that flow, which is why self-knowledge is therapeutic; in Pythagorean terms the virtues are the right intervals of the soul's music. Ethics is regulating the soul toward ἀρετή, which, sustained over time, brings eudaimonia, and like Heracles at the crossroads we choose it, or vice, at every moment.

label: Christmas and the Nativity
take: She reads Christmas as the latest coding of the archetype of the sacred infant, behind which stand the Dionysia and the Heliougenna. She decodes the Nativity line by line: the cave is Plato's Cave, the manger is the solar-plexus seat of the irrational powers, the two animals are spleen and liver, Mary (Despoina) is the soul, Joseph the doubting mind, Herod's soldiers the forces threatening the newborn, and the flight into Egypt keeping it hidden. She ends wishing 'Christougenna, Iliougenna, Alithiougenna': birth of Christ, of the sun, of truth.

label: Science and spirit
take: She respects science absolutely, but when the sciences are studied only materialistically, Platonic epistemology places them among convictions and dogmas; even science can harbour fanaticism, as the medical debates of the previous two years showed. With Kuhn she says communities resist paradigm change from emotional investment, not lack of evidence. The ancient aim is to reunite philosophy's science with its spirituality, 'because the source of science is God who ever geometrises'.

label: The true Self
take: The personality (περσόνα) is the sum of changing parts, a role with its costume and name, and identifying with it is the death philosophy undoes. Life is a theatre: the actor (ἠθοποιός) 'makes an ethos' by how he plays, but is not the role, and the task is to recognise who plays all the roles. Justice as 'doing one's own' refers to the one fiery Self, and acting justly is a two-way road to discovering it. The Titans, our outward tendencies, lock us into a role for every stimulus.

label: The Titans
take: The Titans are not bad guys out there but our inner tendencies: following Proclus she derives the name from τείνω, to stretch or tend. They are the pull of the irrational nature toward externalisation, material and egoic pursuits. Their dismembering of the child Dionysus is daily life fragmenting attention among work, family and taxes, each pull creating a role we lock into, and so the chains of the cave form.

label: The Stoics
take: From the Stoics she takes ἀταραξία, inner peace as the core of εὖ ζῆν, and ἐκπύρωσις, the periodic ignition of the universe in which the seminal reasons (σπερματικοὶ λόγοι) lie as seeds of all forms. Marcus Aurelius, 'very close to my heart this period', teaches ἀπάθεια: happiness not invested in externals, which she distinguishes from indifference, and he shows one can be free even in prison. An unnamed later Stoic gives her the idea that nothing happens to me without my free will.

label: Pythagoras
take: Pythagoras is for her the great initiate who coined the word philosophy and defined its aim as union with the Monad, a 'Greek yoga' that joins the Dionysian, Orphic way of the heart with the Apollonian, Ionian way of mind and science. Arriving between a fading priesthood and a rising science, he reformed Greek tradition, and his highest initiation was political. Above all he is a potential of our own soul: she decodes his name until she can say 'you are Pythagoras'.

label: Harmony
take: Harmony is not the absence of opposites but their sacred union: ἁρμός, a joint, together with κρᾶσις and μῖξις, blending and mixing. With the Pythagoreans she says that without opposition there is no harmony, so we should not fear conflict. Apollo's fourth power, ὁμοπολῶν, moves the poles together into a new unity. In the eros talk, eros is the weft of universal harmony that holds the world in one.

label: Ethos and character
take: Ethics does not mean morality: from ἦθος and ἔθος, habit, it is the habitual way the energy of the soul moves, habits of consciousness. Plato's Academy taught it as moulding oneself into a balanced person, and she notes that ἠθική is an anagram of Ἰθάκη, so knowing the structure of the soul is the way home. Its fullest form is the ethics of love, summed up in the teaching that there are no others.

label: Courageous nobility
take: Courage is a hinge in two talks. In the Ares lesson the awakened need the courage of the spirited part, a virtue of both warrior and philosopher, or the cave will 'eat' them, and the soul needs fearlessness to cross the passage after death. In the 28 October talk the collective «No» of 1940 was possible only because Greeks had cultivated ἀνδρεία in their souls and were brave in daily life, so their bravery could show on the political level.

label: Persephone
take: In her Eleusinian reading Persephone's three names trace three stages of the soul. As 'bearer of death' (φέρουσα φόνον) she descends and lives the death of truth, identification with the body. As Φερσέφασσα, bearer of light, she carries the light that sets her on the path of gestation and stripping. As Φερέπαφα, bearer of touch, she touches the immortal and returns to Mother Demeter.

label: The senses
take: Against the idea that the spiritual must renounce the senses, she teaches that the philosopher purifies them. Sensation (Timaeus 43a-c) is the moment the river's waves, striking the body, reach the soul's circles; the sense organs are only gates, and it was never the body that sensed but the mind. Rightly understood, the senses are sacred gifts for enjoying God and one of the great initiations of embodied life: we reach fullness not through them but with them as allies.

label: Smell and aroma
take: Smell has a special place: it lies between water and air, between sensible and intelligible, and goes straight to memory, so she calls it a direct gate to φρόνησις (which is 'not by chance' akin to ὄσφρησις, smell). Its double nature means a scent can lift the soul (pure flowers, incense, herbs) or drag it down (chemical blends and animal-based perfumes). Incense, θυμίαμα, 'reminds' us (her wordplay) and awakens the soul's Mnemosyne, and whatever we wear and exhale feeds a corresponding order of beings.

label: Love
take: Where eros is the drive toward union, ἀγάπη is the fullness of recognising it. Love is another name for the one, common unity of consciousness, so knowing yourself as love is the single cure for every ill, and love is the beginning of wisdom. Its ethics is concrete: love in word, thought, feeling and act, treating everything as your own household (οἶκος) and doing it selflessly, as Marcus Aurelius taught.

label: Beauty
take: What is beheld at the summit of eros is a κάλλος ἀμήχανον, which she glosses through μηχανή as beauty without mechanism, form or mode, describable only by negation. Beauty is also a mission: the one who returns to the cave raises the sensible to its highest expression of beauty. Greek art's devotion to beauty, symmetry and harmony ('the Acropolis is my witness') shows that the sensible is where the divine expresses its wonder in actuality.

label: Darkness and the descent
take: The winter solstice, the darkest night, is a privileged gate, not a misfortune: darkness means introversion, the time to descend like Persephone into the subconscious with the hero's torch. There you face your monsters, hidden passions and their roots in events, family and ancestors, uproot them and sow virtues. At rock bottom the choice is 'light or nothing', and trauma can become θαῦμα, a miracle.

label: Hellenism
take: Hellenism for her is a universal spirit, not ethnocentric pride, built on two principles: Heraclitus' 'all is one' and 'as above, so below, as within, so without'. Its path was never lost: the golden chain lives in the soul's memory and is allowed again after centuries of bans. In the Pythagoras lesson she tells how a teacher in the Himalayas sent her home: the whole tradition of awakening was already in her own culture.

label: Myth as symbol
take: Myths are theology in the psyche's native symbolic language: mythology is initiation (μύηση) into theology. Homer coded cosmic and karmic laws in analogies, such as Apollo's anger standing for the reaction our actions bring back. Children read such stories literally, which is why Plato filtered tales of jealous or warring gods.

label: Desire and fullness
take: Behind every desire that seeks expression through the senses, the soul is seeking the fullness (κόρος) of the Good, so desire is sacred in its motive. Only wrong education makes it believe fullness lies in one more possession or meal, which breeds the ἀκόρεστον, the insatiable, and explains why many wealthy people are unhappy. What we seek outside is already within, reached by the soul's inward turning (μεταστροφή).

label: The separate self
take: Any identity, even 'the awakened one', sets itself against something else and so keeps a gap between the ego and the pure 'I am', between the ego and the One. She lists the false identities in order: I am my role, then my convictions (left, right, Greek, Platonist), then my knowledge (philosopher, scientist, knower), 'again a trap'. Threatened identity is why scholars and scientific communities resist what they do not understand.

label: Daimon
take: Not the Christian demon but the inner true self, a droplet of God and the inner teacher. She derives it from δαίω, I burn, tying it to Heraclitus's ever-living fire, and from a sense of distributing: each daimon is a localised share of the one fire. Eudaimonia is then that flame touching its own good nature.

label: Zeus
take: Zeus is consciousness in its creative operation, the cosmic mind. His endless loves and children are not literal: goddesses and mortal women are the divine and ordinary ideas that mind mingles with, and every birth is a world. She reads his two names as two movements, Δίας dividing and projecting, Ζεύς unifying and returning (etymologies she offers as her own).

label: Eastern parallels
take: She trained in India and found that meditation there cleared her lens until she could read Plato with new eyes: everything was already in her own tradition. She parallels Greek ideas with the Tao, Atman, Buddha nature and yoga, holding that truth is one. Yet the postwar West's turn East met cultural friction, and a message in the Himalayas told her that what she sought was where she started.

label: Beholding (theasis)
take: θέασις, beholding, is how she says the Greek tradition names awakening: 'the beholding of the One', in which often nothing happens, no gate opens, no angel appears; you simply witness what already is. It shares a root with θέατρον and θεατής: we come into the divine theatre as spectators of truth. Her formula from the Republic is that a change of θέασις (seeing) leads to θέωσις (deification).

label: The apophatic way
take: Because what is realised is ἄρρητον, belonging neither to words nor concepts, she begins by saying what awakening is not: apophatic theology or knowledge. Diotima does the same with absolute beauty (no body, no limbs, no colour). Her practical test follows: while you still see or understand 'something', even God or the light, do not stop; you have not reached Ithaca.

label: Recollection (anamnesis)
take: All knowledge is recollection because the soul's essence is the essence of the cosmos and the divine: knowing is not shopping for something new but activating an imprint already within. Feeling a lack proves it, as you cannot look for keys you do not know you lost. Activating the soul's memory (μνημοσύνη) is, for the ancients, activating eudaimonia; incense 'reminds' us, and her own first reading of Plato at 14 felt like remembering.

label: The Circles of the Same and the Other
take: From the Timaeus and Proclus she teaches that the soul is two circular strips joined in a χ. The Circle of the Same, matching the celestial equator, is the Hestia within that keeps us centred in being; the Circle of the Other, matching the ecliptic and zodiac and divided into seven (she links these to the chakras and planets), carries senses, passions and changing moods. θάτερον is an anagram of θέατρον, the theatre of roles. True human life is their conscious union; equinox and solstice mark their meeting and their greatest distance.

label: Phronesis (practical wisdom)
take: She gives φρόνησις the etymology 'φορᾶς καὶ ῥοῦ νόησις', understanding of motion and flow, the right circular motion of the mind. How far we reach it depends on how we use the senses, on finding the 'algorithm of relationship' between the river's motions and the soul's. Calm (γαλήνη) lets the circles recover so judgment becomes correct, and smell (ὄσφρησις) is 'not by chance' its kin.

label: Matter
take: Matter does not exist apart from consciousness: in the Platonic tradition it is an emanation (ἀπορροή), the last stage of the One's outflowing light, and 'the universe is noetic'. She calls matter-as-primary 'the biggest fake news', an interpretation of consciousness seen at a tilt. Still, the material world is no prison: a provident Demiurge made it as a sacred play of consciousness, and physicists' 'energy soup' is better called an 'energy river'.

label: Eternity and time
take: Following Plato, time is the moving image of eternity, while eternity itself does not move except around itself, like the sun, a sphere or the spinning top of Dionysus. She reads χρόνος as χ (duality) + ῥοή (flow) + νοῦς, from a source the notes cannot identify. In the noetic there is no time; past is memory and future projection. Plotinus' eternity is untrembling (ἀτρεμής), untilted (ἀκλινής) and 'standing in the one'.

label: The Now
take: The only right moment to awaken is now, because you already are That now; saying 'first this, then...' postpones it into a future that is only imagination. The philosophers called νῦν another name of Apollo, pure light, the perfect hour. Solstices and equinoxes can hasten 'the beautiful hour', but the best moment is always now.

label: Telos and entelechy
take: The Greek universe is teleological: nothing is random, and everything tends dynamically toward its purpose, a force that constantly pulls us. Perfection (τελειότητα) is not an abstract ideal but the fulfilment of one's τέλος. Like a seed carrying the whole oak, the soul tends toward eudaimonia because it comes from eudaimonia: our origin is our Ithaca.

label: Aporia (not-knowing)
take: If I do not recognise that I do not know, I do not ask. Admitting not-knowing, Socrates' method, opens the pores (ἀπορία), and then Apollo starts to reveal himself. This is the restlessness of the first step, Pythios, together with the natural appetite (ὀρέγεσθαι) for knowledge that Aristotle describes.

label: Purification
take: Purification runs through her teaching: cathartic virtues (diet, mantras, energy work, cleansing the luminous body that the Chaldean Oracles call the soul's subtle vehicle), Epimenides lifting karma from cities, Diotima cleansing the plague's residue, and tragedy purging audiences through imitation of heroes' passions. Such energetic cleansing, she stresses, is not only an Eastern or New Age idea but is in the Hellenic sources.

label: Life as divine play
take: She calls the phenomenal world a δρώμενον, a sacred enactment, staged within the mind of God, who imagines or dreams it; in this sense it is a phantasm, at once collective and individual. Following Proclus, essence falls into a 'divine sleep' and dreams the many, and death ends the dream. These are her metaphysical views. Practically, the awakened watch the shadow play (she compares it to Karagiozis) while remembering 'I am not this'.

label: Equanimity
take: Following Proclus, she holds that turbulence from the senses can disturb the soul's revolutions but never its essence, so ἀταραξία and ἀπάθεια are not cultivated but revealed. In her own life realisation brought a calm steadiness through both hard and happy events, because happiness came from contact with who she is. This evenness is not apathy: it arrives together with equal love for every being.

label: Worldview (kosmotheasis)
take: She frames whole talks around worldview: the dualist one that splits spirit from matter and humans from nature, and the holistic, unitive Greek one in which sensible and intelligible form a single continuum. Worldview is not academic: she reads the state of the planet as the fruit of a mistaken worldview, and estrangement from natural rhythm as the reason humanity destroys its environment and itself.

label: Measure and the mean
take: The soul's circles run on the mathematical measure that the geometer-God gave them, the ratios of the Timaeus, and violent contact with the river can make them lose it. The centre, the mean (μεσότης), is the hearth of virtue, divine nature and eudaimonia. So she advises not to complain about moderate circumstances: they make the inner equinox, the meeting of the two circles, easier.

label: The Delphic E
take: The cryptic letter E at Delphi, which she attributes, with "Know thyself", to Apollo himself. Of the many readings Plutarch discusses she favours εἶ, "you are", the second person of "I am". Placed beside the precept, it tells the pilgrim that the divinity sought in the temple and in things is what the pilgrim already is.

label: Poseidon
take: Beyond trident and storms, Poseidon is in her reading the higher octave of love, the cohesive force of the universe. His waters are the cosmic ocean that modern cosmologists call the energetic soup, and the Ψ of his trident is the Ψ of ψυχή: souls travelling through the ocean that holds everything together.

label: Athena (the goddess)
take: In the Ares lesson Athena is war 'by union': through providence and strategy she removes the monstrous and passionate so that beings reunite, using every other means before bloody war, and she always overpowers Ares because wisdom rules force. In the radio interview she names wisdom as the goddess's first virtue, joined by justice, temperance and discernment. Her birth from Zeus's head means wisdom is the fruiting (κάρπισμα) of mind, its τέλος.

label: Philotes, cosmic love
take: The Presocratic, above all Empedoclean, name for the cohesive, attractive force that makes the many into one universe; Empedocles said everything is ruled by attraction and repulsion, as physics now says too. To know ourselves as cosmic φιλότης is, for her, the panacea for separateness. Self-knowledge leads to it, and from it comes the Neoplatonic call to love all things.

label: The idiotes
take: In ancient Greece whoever cut himself off from the whole ('what do I care what society does') was an ἰδιώτης, and English kept the word as 'idiot'. She reads ἠλίθιος not as an insult but as a cognitive state: one who lives 'in lethe', having forgotten he is one with his fellow citizens and with everything. He sees himself as a little seashell in the ocean of the absolute, and she calls this a personal and collective disease of Greek society.

label: Eutychia, good fortune
take: Good fortune from circumstances: real but circular and impermanent, a turning wheel that can easily become misfortune. Someone with every material good who has not found the hearth of the soul can feel fortune for a while but never eudaimonia. Covid, she says, exposed how external foundations betray us.

label: Entelechy
take: She glosses Aristotle's word as the τέλος we have (ἔχειν) within (ἐν). As an olive seed carries the blossoming, fruiting olive tree, the soul carries the end for which it incarnated, and that end is εὐδαιμονία. In the 28 October talk the human entelechy is to attune one's existence to the Good, and she uses it against the social-contract view: our inner end is goodness, not wickedness.

label: Gnosis
take: One of the four names of philosophy's goal: non-dual awareness that rises beyond phenomena and duality to realise what is already whole and divine. It is freedom-giving knowledge, and she calls the final stage of Hellenic meditation, where subject and object merge, the very meaning of gnosis.

label: Theoria, the View
take: She reads θεωρία as θεός plus ὁρῶ, I see the god: Plotinus's View, the vision at the end of the path. It is indescribable Beauty and ineffable luminosity, unsayable because words work in duality. In her three-stage meditation it appears to be the final stage, where no subject contemplates an object.

label: Hellenic meditation
take: She presents a native Greek meditation path, not borrowed yoga: focused contemplation (στοχασμός), expansive inner dialogue of awareness (διαλογισμός), then non-dual gazing. Elsewhere she teaches Pythagorean Hellenic mindfulness, studying one's motivations before, during and after each act, and guides an ether meditation on the space of awareness. Its structures, she says, can be drawn out of texts such as the cave.

label: Experience and the infinite
take: Realisation is not an experience: ἐμπειρία belongs to πέρας, the bounded, and the infinite has no contour to be experienced. We do not experience the infinite, we are it, focused into a local point (Hestia). The point of view of that localisation is a μοίρα, a word that also means fate, so our destiny is the perspective of the local mind.

label: Symbol and archetype
take: A symbol carries something sensible (a king sailing to Troy and back) up to the intelligible level of the laws of human and cosmic nature. Jung's archetype is, in her view, a renaming of this Greek idea. Tragedy proves the point, since only living archetypes could produce catharsis; and for Greeks the Odyssey is a symbol, while Hollywood treats it as merchandise.

label: Homer
take: The Homeric epics were the pillars of Greekness and the source of tragedy's archetypes; Homer may even be the title of a rhapsode rather than one person. Plato gave a whole book of the Republic to Homer and filtered his literal-sounding stories, since Homer coded cosmic laws in analogies. Healing, for Greeks, means bending over Homer's spring again to drink the water of Mnemosyne.

label: Ithaca and nostos
take: Νόστος, Odysseus' sweet homecoming, is what gives life its νοστιμιά, its flavour, and its eudaimonia. Yet arrival is not completion: Odysseus reaches Ithaca only mid-Odyssey and must still face the suitors, which she tentatively reads as our illusions, just as the freed prisoner returns to the cave. In the 28 October talk Ἰθάκη is an anagram of ἠθική: the passions toss us on stormy seas and make us lose our Ithaca, so coming home is ethics. With Cavafy, we meet the monsters on the way only if we carry them in our soul.

label: Plato's Republic
take: She calls it Plato's magnum opus: if all his other works were lost, its quintessence would survive in it. Subtitled 'On the Just', it begins in Piraeus with the question of justice and covers soul, virtues, constitutions, music, education, epistemology and life after death. It must be read whole, not in excerpts, and its core thesis is that the just city cannot exist outside unless it is first built in the soul.

label: The golden thread and its cut
take: She traces one lineage from Orpheus (an avatar and son of the Muses who founded the mysteries) through the Presocratics, Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, the Stoics and the Neoplatonists, ended when Justinian closed the schools in 529 AD on pain of death. The church kept the logic, cosmology and ethics but erased the practices, leaving a dissected corpus of texts without methods. The spirit went underground and, she says, is now being rekindled in Greece as an indigenous path.

label: Spirituality and religion
take: She warns that spiritual people have been trained to be 'lukewarm water', soft and guilty about strength, and calls this a cave strategy to disarm awakening. Strong traditions (Greek, Hindu, Tibetan, Native American) pair the illuminated one with the warrior, and only declining traditions undermine the warrior. The more refined we are inside, the firmer we must be outside, and spiritual work is incomplete until it becomes action and life.

label: The divine and the gods
take: There are three ways to approach any god, text or idea, all true at once: external, at the πρόναος ('I am here, Apollo is there'); internal, Orphic, where the god becomes a power of my soul; and central, mysteriac, where the god is lived as an active mode of being of the One. The god appears differently according to the seeker's tuning. θέασις contains θεός and θεά, so beholding is meeting the divine that is already here.

label: The Greek language
take: Greek is a performative, vibratory language: like Beethoven or a mantra it cannot truly be translated, and reading it in the original acts on soul and energy. Following the Cratylus and Proclus she holds that letters and words encode movements of being, so a teaching can be drawn out of a single word. Her talks are full of such indigenous etymologies, which she admits grammarians may contest.

label: Music and the Muses
take: Music is Apollo's fourth power and, for her, the art of harmonising opposites rather than playing an instrument. Socrates' daimonion told him 'make music and work at it', which she reads as reaching the last Apollonian step: having gone beyond the poles, return to the many and harmonise them. Like the freed prisoner going back into the cave, the philosopher must make music with others, which she calls the political step of consciousness. The aim is a stable, virtuous, 'musical' life.

label: Psycho-politics
take: Political regimes, she argues, match the psychic state of the people. When the desiring part (ἐπιθυμητικόν), fed by consumerism and advertising, seizes the reins from the heart's beat for freedom and the capacity for knowledge, a people gets an 'oligarchic tyranny' that calls itself democracy. So the first polity to govern is one's own soul: without self-mastery, from what position would you govern others?

label: Ignorance as separateness
take: The prisoners' defining mark is double ignorance: they do not know that they do not know, and take the cave for life itself. Worse still is to believe you know. Such people call the spiritual seeker mad and later persecute those who return to free them; Plato defines paideia against ἀμάθεια, the state of not-learning.

label: Crisis
take: Eras of crisis, she says, have always been more fertile for conceiving the seed of change: transformations follow a crisis. In the radio interview she reads the pandemic, harsh as it was, as a 'blessing' that forced the turning inward on everyone at once, as if life itself made us practise asceticism together and ask where the basis of our well-being lies. These are her interpretations of the crisis, offered as a spiritual reading. In the 28 October talk she warns that a force for change with no rooted values is soon swallowed by the old system.

label: The feminine in philosophy
take: Her Harvard research reclaims the feminine in two ways: historically, recovering forgotten women who shaped philosophy beyond Hypatia and Diotima, and epistemologically. Academia formed its methods when women were excluded, so its norms stay masculine and sideline emotion and psychology in knowing. The deeper call is a holistic education of mind, heart and ἦθος.

label: Fence of Olympus
take: Her favourite line of the hymn calls Ares the ἕρκος Ὀλύμπου, the fence or fortress of Olympus. She pictures him as the line of shields around the gods and as the outer electron shell around Hestia's nucleus: the outermost layer is the most exposed, which is why the myths show him straying and switching sides. Spiritually it means our centre is wisdom but our edges must be red, because creation, the soul and awakening all need guarded boundaries; she also links ὅρκος, the oath, to setting a boundary.

label: Practice of death
take: Her second definition of philosophy comes from the Phaedo: the philosopher accomplishes in life what fate accomplishes for everyone at death, the release of the soul from the body. She stresses that this means dis-identifying from the body, not leaving it, and that touching truth and dying are the same thing. She often quotes a modern teacher: if you die before you die, you will not die when you die.

label: Orpheus
take: In the Ares lesson Orpheus is the author of the hymn cycle, and the order of its last five hymns is itself a teaching. In the Pythagoras lesson she reads ΟΡΦΕΑΣ as an anagram of ΦΟΡΕΑΣ, the carrier of the flowing light, a first 'avatar' bearing Athena's primordial wisdom. The Orphic current is the heart-centred, ecstatic, Dionysian way that had degenerated by Pythagoras' time and that he reformed, and the Orphic teachers place the soul's memory in the ἦτορ, the spiritual heart.

label: Know the knower
take: Her deepest reading of self-knowledge is to turn consciousness back on itself and ask who the one who knows is. You find no someone and no something, only boundlessness (ἀπεραντοσύνη), freedom, timelessness, calm and peace. This consciousness is the stable basis of every experience, pure knowing that knows itself and that, through its modifications, made the appearance of the many. She calls it easy, a meditation one can do now and repeat.

label: Dis-identification
take: Her own word for the Platonic separation of soul from body is αποταύτιση, dis-identification: not leaving the body but ceasing to take it for oneself. You have a body, emotions, desires and thoughts that change from age five to a hundred, while the 'I am' stays. Its fruit is freedom from the illusion of a self bounded by the skin, and in the radio interview it appears as undressing the roles and labels (name, profession, parent, nationality) that cripple the divine self.

label: Truth by subtraction
take: Truth, for her, is a subtractive process. You need to acquire nothing, because the soul already carries the seeds of eudaimonia, knowledge and freedom and is 'baptised in the light of wisdom'; you only remove what covers it. On the radio she pictures it as a flower opening petal by petal as we shed roles. In the 28 October talk every subtraction is a «No», which is why the national «No» stirs Greeks, though a «No» must then be completed by a «Yes».

label: Aletheia, unforgetting
take: She reads ἀλήθεια as alpha privative plus λήθη: truth is the lifting of forgetfulness. This fits Plato's teaching that knowledge is recollection, so knowing is activating what we already carry, not conquering something foreign, which she calls one of the most distinctive features of the Greek view. In the Pythagoras lesson she adds an anagram: ἀλήθεια and θήλεια, the female, so truth is always gestating and giving birth.

label: Touching truth
take: For the ancients, she says, philosophy's goal was to touch (ἐφάπτεσθαι) the truth experientially, not to master arguments. The touch is as tangible as touch, the heaviest sense, yet as dimensionless as Euclid's point. Since ἅπτω also means to kindle (think of a lighter, αναπτήρας), touching truth sets the whole being ablaze and rekindles the inner fire, contact with Heraclitus' ever-living fire.

label: Union with the Monad
take: Ἕνωσις with the Monad is Pythagoras' name for what others call yoga, 'union', or nirvana, and for her it is the aim of philosophy. It is not reaching something far away but realising, with mind, heart and body, that you and the cosmic ocean are already one. The final step of the Pythagorean school, ὁμοίωσις θεῷ, is the same awakening: my essence and the universe's essence are one.

label: Work and action
take: Awakening must become work. After 'make music' comes 'and work': like the freed prisoner who goes back down, the realised one builds the insight into a way of life, which is why the highest Pythagorean initiation was political. She glosses ἔργον as ἔρωτος γόνος, offspring of eros. In the Ares lesson all work and industriousness run on Arean energy, 'the moment I stand up', and truth not expressed in action is incomplete truth.

label: The Golden Verses
take: She describes the Golden Verses as 72 verses taught for a thousand years as the first lesson of the Platonic school, to be listened to as a vibration, not only as information. She reads their last lines as 'if' you leave the body, not 'when': leaving the body at death is not liberation, dropping the illusion that you are the body is. Their promise, 'an immortal god, no longer mortal', means you do not become immortal; you realise you always were.

label: Immortality
take: She separates two immortalities. The soul's immortality 'we already have'. The hero's immortality is a state of consciousness: defying death means not caring for one's own hide, so one dis-identifies from the ego, becomes one with the all, and since the all always is, how could one die? She reads βροτός, mortal, as 'eaten' (as in 'this problem is eating me'), so ἄμβροτος is the un-consumed, imperishable.

label: What is a Hellene
take: For her 'Hellene' is a level of the soul, not an ethnicity or a seed asleep in the DNA: an existential, cultural and spiritual achievement. She reads the name through 'Ἑλ', which she takes as spiritual light, so a Hellene is one who tunes his mind to that light, and since light knows no borders a Hellene cannot look after his own interest alone. Many Greeks, she says, are Hellenes in potential (ἐν δυνάμει) but not in actuality (ἐν ἐνεργείᾳ); in 1940 they were Hellenes in actuality.

label: Ancient as a quality
take: To fulfil the heritage, she says, we must become ancients ourselves, with no regressive intent. 'Ancient' is not a date but a quality: a being's position toward the ἀρχαί, the value principles, and toward the first ἀρχή, which some call God, others the first cause (πρωταίτιον), and our philosophers the Good.

label: The «No» and the «Yes»
take: She reads the «No» of 28 October 1940 as a philosophical lesson. Every subtraction on the path is a «No», said first within, which is why the national «No» stirs every Greek. But a «No» without a «Yes» is lame: a reaction stays locked to the action it opposes and carries the seeds of its perpetuation. The «Yes» is cultivation, the soil, water and pruning that let the seed of «No» sprout, and the two must cycle forever.

label: As above, so below
take: The second principle of Hellenism in her 28 October talk: what is above is like what is below, and what is within is like what is without, so there is continuity across all scales. She says it was in a sense given by the Greeks to the Egyptians and engraved on an emerald tablet, which she offers as her account. In Plato it becomes the mirroring of soul and polity, and in the Ares lesson the same law makes the force behind outer law a model for the soul.

label: Political eros
take: Against the modern foundation of politics on fear, she proposes the ancient one: political eros. It carries a positive sign of hope and love, and it is the summit of Diotima's ascent, an eros that rises beyond a beautiful body and soul to embrace the whole city: its nature, trees, buildings, citizens, institutions and laws. Since eros is activated by the καλόν, we must make ourselves lovable: be the change.

label: Cultivation
take: The word 'cultivation' is used for only two human activities, she notes: tilling the earth and tending the soul, so soul and earth are strangely identified. The soul needs good seed, good soil and continuous care in rhythm with nature's turns, as good farmers sow by the stars. Virtues make the soul gentle and fertile so it can receive the seed of spirit, and the «Yes» that completes the «No» is exactly this cultivation, with Demeter's help.

label: The three parts of the soul
take: She uses Plato's three parts of the soul in four talks: the desiring part, the spirited part, which she equates with the heart and emotions, and the reasoning part. Studying them is the first, valid stage of self-knowledge and an 'extremely therapeutic' practice of observation. But they are powers of the soul, not the soul: as the melody is not the kithara, the maker is not the made. Politically, when desire takes the reins, a people's regime turns tyrannical.

label: Acceptance and the ἔστω
take: For hard times she offers a mathematician's tool. As a proof starts from 'ἔστω', 'let it be so', one can take as a working hypothesis that everything is perfect and just and must happen for some reason, since from partway up the mountain we cannot see all the folds. Saying 'let it be' is acceptance, an attitude of mind and heart; because the ego is a form of resistance, each acceptance opens us to the Whole.

label: Gratitude and thanksgiving
take: She ends her lessons with gratitude. Εὐγνωμοσύνη contains γνώμων, a gauge: it is the measure that immediately activates the εὖ, the good and divine nature. It is a heart virtue that aligns the spirited part with the soul's purpose and 'leads the soul' toward its entelechy. Εὐχαριστία, from εὖ and χάρις, activates grace, the touch of the Three Graces or the right conjuncture, the incalculable factor that, with our own effort, completes eudaimonia.

label: Mantic knowing
take: Μαντική for her is not laurel-chewing or tripods but unmediated knowledge, reached in inner silence rather than by reading, being told or proving. It comes from divine μανία, which she reads as the sacred marriage of heart and nous, not madness. It is Apollo's second power (ἁπλοῦς): removing the many judgements reveals a simple truth, and 'each of us is a seer'. The great ideas of Einstein, Planck, Heisenberg and Tesla came this way, in flashes, with proofs later.

label: Plutarch
take: In On the E at Delphi Plutarch gives the five cult names of Apollo, learned from his teacher Ammonius, each matched to the seeker's condition; she reads them as five steps of awakening. He also treats Apollo and Dionysus as one, two states of the universe: the One becoming many and the many returning in a luminous, non-material fire. She departs from him in one place: he groups Delios and Phanaios together, while she makes them two separate steps.

label: Plato's Cratylus
take: In the Cratylus Socrates gives four etymologies of Apollo's name matching his four powers: medicine (ἀπολούων), mantic (ἁπλοῦς), archery (ἀεὶ βάλλων) and music (ὁμοπολῶν). She uses them as the four passages between Plutarch's five names, since five steps have four intervals. She also takes from it the principle that letters can interchange and similar words share meaning, which licenses her wordplay.

label: Health and healing
take: Apollo's first power is healing: father of Asclepius, he heals through light and pure vision. Greek medicine is holistic, illness starting in spirit or nous, then soul, then body; illness is complication and health is simplicity and a mean, with the noetic idea as the stable centre. In the eros talk, living in the flow of eros gives ῥῶσις, vigour, and with Socrates health is inner peace while illness is an inner civil war. Healing begins with the will to change.

label: Steady will
take: Healing starts with ρ, the intention and will to change: 'you must want to change', otherwise nothing moves. At the archer's step (ἀεὶ βάλλων) the will stops changing and holds one target; every traveller must choose one direction, vice or virtue, and carry it through, avoiding πολυπραγμοσύνη. Stabilising flashes of awakening into a way of life needs this steady will, like a diamond made of one element.

label: The ennead
take: Four etymologies plus five names make nine keys, and she reads the ennead as νέα ἑνάς, 'the new one'. It names the new unity that appears when Apollo, having gone beyond the poles, harmonises the many again. She ties this reading to the Pythagoreans.

label: Dialogue
take: At the fifth step, Leschenorios, Plutarch's seekers 'are active and enjoy using dialogue and philosophising with one another'. The λέσχη (from λέγω) was the place where initiates gathered, there was one at Delphi, and 'we are a lesche'. Shared dialogue is how a community lives devoted to knowledge, truth and the common good, as in the ancient philosophical schools.

label: Peace
take: She derives εἰρήνη from εἴρω, to join, the same root she finds in ἔρως, so 'peace and eros are two sides of the same coin'. Health is a form of inner peace and illness an inner civil war (στάσις), in the psyche and in society alike. Apollo's archery is 'a war of peace, of light' that in the end is not war: wildness touching a focused will is tamed.

label: Aphrodite
take: She recalls the two Aphrodites of Greek tradition: Οὐρανία, eros 'from here upward' through pure emotion and spirit, and Πάνδημος, eros approached in a lustful, bodily way. She uses the pair to suggest that societies promote different qualities of eros and could be studied that way.

label: Silence
take: Mantic, unmediated knowledge is reached in inner silence. Without analysing, one lets an answer or awareness appear and trusts the intuition the heart speaks first, then the mind.

label: The divided line
take: She reads the Line as the ordering of what the Sun taught: five objects of seeing or thinking and five modes of consciousness, from conjecture and opinion inside the cave, through knowledge of concepts and of numbers above it, to union with the Good at its top. She stresses that she decodes these five from the text rather than adding them, and that they match Plato's five levels of being, the five constitutions and the Pythagorean pentagram. The line is drawn in the mean and extreme ratio, φ.

label: The golden ratio φ
take: The Line is constructed in the mean and extreme ratio, a formulation of φ, which she calls 'the rhythm of harmony', found in the Acropolis, flowers, shells, galaxies and the human body. Because every level relates to every higher one by the same ratio, φ is 'the magic key of justice', the harmony of all levels.

label: Conjecture (eikasia)
take: The lowest mode of mind, when intellection turns to images and shadows. She reads the shadows psychologically: the shadows of the personality, traumas and the projections we cast on others, as when a partner's morning frown becomes 'he doesn't love me'. This is where psychology and Jung's shadow work come in.

label: Opinion and conviction
take: When we turn to sensible objects we form opinions, beliefs and views, the 'my view and your view' prized in democracy, and she places them inside the cave, in what she calls the deep cave. They rest on the belief 'I am the body and others are bodies'. A conviction is an opinion clothed in emotion, which is why even science, studied only materialistically, can turn into dogma and fanaticism, as Kuhn saw with paradigms.

label: The wonder-workers
take: Outwardly they are all who build a mass reality: television, the news, the models people are told to believe. But while everyone wants to catch the outer wonder-workers, she turns inward: the true wonder-worker is the nous itself. Most people, she says with Plato, run through the wonder-worker: 'I have a view and I believe it.'

label: The Horai and the soul's ripe hour
take: Her own gate out of the cave is the ripeness of the soul: the hour has come, as chamomile springs up in spring once all the conditions are met. Since the talk is about justice, she notes that the Horai are the first daughters of Zeus by Themis, goddess of justice, and that their sisters the Graces name the same moment as grace. She says she is writing a treatise on the Horai.

label: Illusion and interpretation
take: She refuses to call life an illusion, since then the Good would have created something false; illusion is produced by interpretation, the way our nous works. The greatest illusion of the spiritual scene is 'the awakened subject'. After the return she says even illusion is awakening that forgets itself.

label: The new spiritual cave
take: Her name for the 'renovation of the cave' produced by today's inflation of spiritual terms: awakening approached materialistically, what other traditions call spiritual materialism, with wonder-mongering and misinformation. Identities such as 'the awakened one', or a spirituality fenced by race, are further versions of it.

label: Participation (methexis)
take: Her word for the final stage of the Line and of the ascent: participation in, or union with, the One, the Good, after one has already come to know ideas and numbers. She reads the Symposium's formless final spectacle as this μέθεξις. With Plotinus she adds that in the end 'there was not even union', since one was always the One.

label: Observing the mind
take: What is now called mindfulness, she says, is the path of self-knowledge: recognising at each moment how your mind works, noticing when you conjecture and when you simply hold an opinion and believe it. Learning to function without the mediation of views, dogmas and convictions is where one begins to leave the cave. Her book in progress, based on her course on the cave, focuses on this.

label: Hermes
take: Those freed who go back into the cave to help lead her to the epithet ψυχοπομπός, guide of souls, belonging to Hermes, 'the symbol of the teacher who unites the two worlds'. With his caduceus he leads Persephone back to Demeter in spring. Crossing the dark valley, one needs a good psychopomp.

label: Reincarnation
take: Taking up the host's point that souls may have lived in East and West, she says the passer-by of another ethnicity could be Aristotle reborn, so racial distinctions miss the soul. She notes that Book X of the Republic teaches metempsychosis, and mocks the academic view that Plato 'got tired' and threw in the myth of Er.

label: Enlightenment
take: She uses φώτισις nearly interchangeably with awakening for the completion at the top of the line. Her criterion: as long as you say 'I am the enlightened one', it is not complete. The true state is Οὖτις, Odysseus's 'Nobody', which Plotinus calls silence and Buddhists the luminous void.

label: The heroic path
take: In Athena's reading the hero is not a romantic figure but a stage in the evolution of consciousness, as Plato and later Platonism describe it. Human consciousness turns in the cycle of days; then suddenly something pushes, and a spark of eros lights, eros in the ontological sense: 'this does not fill me, I want my freedom'. From there begin the labours (ἆθλοι) needed to find who one is at one's centre, like Theseus going to the heart of the labyrinth. Ἥρως comes from ἔρως, so without eros there is no heroic path.

label: One's own work
take: To young people asking what to study and to adults whose fire has gone out, Athena gives the same answer: come to your centre, listen to your heart and ask what you love to do. The ancients held that every soul is born with a mission, its οἰκεῖον ἔργον, the work closest and warmest to its heart; doing what is one's own is οἰκειοπραγία. Fulfil it and you feel full and εὐδαίμων. Athena's two criteria: you burn with zeal for it, and while doing it you lose the sense of time, because love works in eternity.

label: Faith (pistis)
take: For Athena faith is not the opposite of knowledge but a necessary step towards it, a 'scientific stage' found in the theory of knowledge of Plato's Republic: the interval between ignorance and knowledge. To believe (πιστεύω) is to give credit (πίστωση) that something may be so, as a scientist believes a new theory possible before shutting himself in the lab to prove it; that is why πίστη sits inside the word ἐπιστήμη. Faith in the good is the voice of Mnemosyne in us, an inner knowing that our nature, like the nature of the universe, is the Good.
